stem:
A 1-month-old boy is found to have a congenital absence of the thymus.

Which of the following cell populations would be most directly depleted by this defect, given where it normally completes its maturation?

options.label: A
options.misconception: None; T cells mature in the thymus.
options.explanation: Although both B and T cells initially develop from bone marrow, T cells migrate to the thymus gland where they further mature; without a thymus this maturation cannot occur.

options.label: B
options.misconception: A myeloid granulocyte is being tied to a lymphoid organ.
options.explanation: Neutrophils mature entirely within the myeloid lineage in bone marrow; thymic absence affects the T-lymphocyte line.

options.label: C
options.misconception: The two lymphocyte maturation sites are being interchanged.
options.explanation: B cells mature in red bone marrow, not the thymus, so a thymic defect spares their maturation while crippling T-cell production.

options.label: D
options.misconception: The platelet precursor is being assigned thymic maturation.
options.explanation: Megakaryocytes develop and remain in bone marrow; the thymus is the maturation site for T cells only.

options.label: E
options.misconception: A myeloid phagocyte precursor is being linked to the thymus.
options.explanation: Monocytes arise from myeloid stem cells in marrow and mature into macrophages in tissues; they do not depend on the thymus.

context: Learning objective: map lymphocyte maturation sites. All lymphocytes arise from lymphoid stem cells in bone marrow, but maturation splits: B cells mature in red bone marrow while T cells migrate to the thymus — the anatomical basis for the cellular-immunity defect of thymic aplasia (DiGeorge).
